EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  

====================================================================  
1. Identification Strategy  
--------------------------------------------------------------------  
Method:  Staggered Difference-in-Differences (DID) complemented by an event-study specification.  

Rationale  
• The intrastate branching deregulations occur at different years across states but are discrete, well-dated shocks.  
• The panel covers many pre- and post-years, letting us compare changes in growth inside a state before vs. after deregulation to changes in states that have not yet (or never) deregulated.  
• The rich set of state and year fixed effects absorbs all time-invariant state factors and nation-wide macro shocks.  
• An event study around the reform date transparently tests the parallel-trend assumption and illustrates dynamic effects.  
• Recent econometric advances (e.g., Callaway-Sant’Anna 2021; Sun & Abraham 2021) correct the bias that arises in traditional TWFE DID with staggered timing, so we will implement these estimators.  

Optional robustness extensions  
• Border-county triple-differences to rule out cross-state spillovers.  
• Synthetic-control or Matrix Completion as placebo checks for high-leverage states.  


====================================================================  
2. Treatment and Control  
--------------------------------------------------------------------  
Treatment variable  
  Treated = 1 for state-year observations in which the state has already lifted intrastate branching restrictions (and remains 1 thereafter).  

Control group  
  All state-year observations where the state has not yet deregulated by that year serve as the contemporaneous control.  
  – States that never deregulate by 1994 contribute control observations for the whole sample.  
  – States that deregulate later act as controls until the year before their own reform (“not-yet-treated”).  

Treatment timing / event date  
  Year 0 = first calendar year in which the statewide removal of branching restrictions became effective (coded from legislative enactment dates).  
  Event-time dummies (k = –10,…,+10) for the event study; years outside this window are binned.  

Running variable / cutoff  
  Not applicable (no RDD).  


====================================================================  
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
--------------------------------------------------------------------  
A1. Parallel Pre-Trends  
  In absence of deregulation, treated and control states would have followed similar trajectories in per-capita income/output growth.  
  Plausibility:  Regulations were primarily altered for political/technological reasons; many papers document no systematic pre-trend in state growth around these reforms.  

A2. No Anticipation  
  Economic growth does not jump before the law takes effect because agents cannot perfectly time or front-run the reform.  
  Plausibility:  Implementation often required several months of regulatory writing; still, we will check for statistically significant leads.  

A3. Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA)  
  A state’s growth is affected by its own deregulation, not directly by another state’s.  
  Plausibility:  Some cross-border lending could contaminate neighbors; we will test for spillovers with border-state dummies / triple-diff.  

A4. Exogeneity of Reform Timing  
  Conditional on fixed effects and controls, the exact year a state deregulates is as-good-as-random with respect to contemporaneous economic conditions.  
  Plausibility:  Prior literature attributes timing to politics and technology diffusion (ATM networks, legal suits). We will control for state political variables and initial conditions.  

A5. No Concurrent State-Specific Shocks  
  No other major policy or shock coincides with the reform in a way that differentially affects treated states.  
  Plausibility:  We will include controls for other deregulations (interstate branching, usury laws, tax changes) and interact them with time.  


====================================================================  
4. Threats to Identification & Remedies  
--------------------------------------------------------------------  
T1. Endogenous Timing / Reverse Causality  
  States with slowing growth might deregulate to stimulate the economy.  
  • Examine pre-trend coefficients in event study; should be flat.  
  • Use political instruments (e.g., party of governor × election cycle) in IV robustness.  
  • Control for lagged growth rates and state political variables.  

T2. Spillovers Across States  
  A bank headquartered in a deregulated state can lend in neighboring regulated states, contaminating controls.  
  • Add border-state-year observations and include “neighbor treated” indicator.  
  • Re-estimate after dropping border states or using within-state county data where possible.  

T3. Other Financial Deregulations  
  Many states simultaneously lifted interstate restrictions or changed usury ceilings.  
  • Include dummies for interstate branching, M&A liberalizations, and interest-rate deregulations, each interacted with post periods.  
  • Alternatively, limit sample to years before interstate deregulation wave (e.g., end in 1990) as robustness.  


====================================================================  
5. R Code Outline (executable)  
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages -------------------------------------------------------
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)        # for high-dim fixed effects
library(did)           # Callaway & Sant’Anna staggered DID
library(broom)         # tidying
options(fixest_progress = FALSE)

# 1. Load Data ------------------------------------------------------
# Assume three CSV files: growth.csv, banking.csv, controls.csv
growth   <- read_csv("data/growth.csv")     # state, year, rgsp_pc_growth, rincome_pc_growth
banking  <- read_csv("data/banking.csv")    # state, year, charge_offs, npl, loan_rate
controls <- read_csv("data/controls.csv")   # state, year, init_income, schooling, dereg_year

panel <- growth %>%
  left_join(banking,  by = c("state","year")) %>%
  left_join(controls, by = c("state","year"))

# 2. Construct Key Variables ---------------------------------------
panel <- panel %>%
  group_by(state) %>%
  mutate(treat       = if_else(year >= dereg_year, 1L, 0L),
         years_since = year - dereg_year,                          # event time
         post        = (year >= dereg_year) & !is.na(dereg_year),
         never_treat = is.na(dereg_year)) %>%
  ungroup()

# 3. Main TWFE DID --------------------------------------------------
twfe <- feols(rgsp_pc_growth ~ treat | state + year,
              data = panel, cluster = "state")
summary(twfe)

# 4. Callaway & Sant’Anna Estimator --------------------------------
cs <- att_gt(yname   = "rgsp_pc_growth",
             gname   = "dereg_year",            # first treatment year
             idname  = "state",
             tname   = "year",
             xformla = ~ init_income + schooling,
             data    = panel,
             panel   = TRUE)
agg_effect <- aggte(cs, type = "group")         # overall ATT
summary(agg_effect)
ggdid(cs)                                        # event-study plot

# 5. Robustness Check: Leads & Lags -------------------------------
panel <- panel %>%
  mutate(lag2 = lag(treat, 2),
         lag1 = lag(treat, 1),
         lead1= lead(treat, 1),
         lead2= lead(treat, 2))

leadlag <- feols(rgsp_pc_growth ~ lag2 + lag1 + treat + lead1 + lead2 |
                   state + year, data = panel, cluster = "state")
etable(leadlag, drop = "year|state")

# 6. Robustness Check: Border Omission -----------------------------
border_states <- read_csv("data/border_states.csv")   # neighbors to ever-treated states
panel_nb <- panel %>% filter(!state %in% border_states$state)

twfe_nb <- feols(rgsp_pc_growth ~ treat | state + year,
                 data = panel_nb, cluster = "state")
summary(twfe_nb)
```

====================================================================  
6. Expected Results  
--------------------------------------------------------------------  
Theory: Better screening/monitoring reallocates credit to higher productivity firms → faster TFP growth → higher aggregate income per capita.  

Prior sign: Positive.  

Ballpark magnitude: Classic estimates (Jayaratne & Strahan 1996) suggest ~0.4–0.6 ppt increase in annual real per-capita income growth. Hence I expect roughly +0.5 percentage points in our sample, equivalent to about a 10–15 % acceleration relative to the 1970–90 average growth rate of 3–4 % per year.  


====================================================================  
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)  
--------------------------------------------------------------------  
C1: Pre-treatment parallel trends clearly demonstrated by event-study …… 1  
C2: No anticipation (leads insignificant) ………………………………………… 1  
C3: Exogeneity of reform timing (robust to political controls) …………… 0.8  
C4: No spillovers (border-state tests inconclusive) ………………………… 0.6  
C5: Correct estimator for staggered timing (CS/Sun-Abraham) …………… 1  
Overall average ≈ 0.88 → Reasonably credible though spillovers remain a concern.
